title: Look anything up with XLOOKUP
goal: You will replace legacy VLOOKUP formulas with exact-match, fallback, and two-way XLOOKUP formulas in a working Excel sheet.
prerequisites: An Excel workbook containing VLOOKUP formulas
A lookup table with unique IDs in its first column
A row-and-column table for the two-way lookup

steps.action: Duplicate the worksheet that contains the VLOOKUP formulas.
steps.where: Worksheet tab bar at the bottom of the Excel window.
steps.why: A copy preserves the original formulas for comparison and recovery.
steps.checkpoint: A second worksheet tab appears with the same data as the original.
hint_levels: Start with the sheet tab you plan to edit.
The tab's context menu includes an option for copying the entire worksheet.
Right-click the worksheet tab, click Move or Copy, select Create a copy, and click OK.

steps.action: Select the first cell containing a VLOOKUP formula.
steps.where: Home tab > Editing group > Find & Select > Find.
steps.why: Starting with a real legacy formula makes the conversion directly applicable to your workbook.
steps.checkpoint: The selected cell's formula bar begins with =VLOOKUP(.
hint_levels: Search the sheet's formulas for the old function name.
Use Find with Look in set to Formulas so Excel searches formulas instead of displayed values.
Press Ctrl+F, enter VLOOKUP, click Options, choose Formulas under Look in, and click Find Next.

steps.action: Replace the selected VLOOKUP with an XLOOKUP that uses the same lookup cell, key column, and return column.
steps.where: Formula bar above the worksheet grid.
steps.why: XLOOKUP separates the lookup and return ranges and performs exact matching by default.
steps.checkpoint: The cell displays the same result as before and the formula bar begins with =XLOOKUP(.
hint_levels: Map the old formula's lookup value and table columns into XLOOKUP.
Use =XLOOKUP(lookup_value,lookup_column,return_column), choosing the old table's first column as the lookup column and its returned column as the return column.
Click the formula bar, enter =XLOOKUP(original_lookup_cell,original_key_range,original_return_range), and press Enter.

steps.action: Add a readable fallback as the fourth XLOOKUP argument.
steps.where: Formula bar for the converted result cell.
steps.why: The if-not-found argument replaces #N/A with a message users can act on.
steps.checkpoint: The formula bar shows "Not found" as the fourth argument.
hint_levels: Look immediately after the return array.
XLOOKUP's fourth argument is the value displayed when no exact match exists.
Edit the formula to =XLOOKUP(lookup_value,lookup_column,return_column,"Not found") and press Enter.

steps.action: Temporarily enter a nonexistent lookup value in the input cell referenced by the formula.
steps.where: Referenced lookup-value cell in the worksheet grid.
steps.why: Testing a missing key proves that the fallback handles failed matches.
steps.checkpoint: The XLOOKUP result cell displays Not found instead of #N/A.
hint_levels: Use a value that cannot appear in the key column.
Replace the current lookup ID with a clearly fake value such as TEST-999.
Select the lookup input cell, type TEST-999, and press Enter.

steps.action: Restore the original lookup value in the input cell.
steps.where: Quick Access Toolbar > Undo, or the worksheet grid.
steps.why: Restoring the valid key leaves the workbook ready for normal use.
steps.checkpoint: The result changes from Not found back to the expected matched value.
hint_levels: Reverse only the temporary test entry.
Undo returns the input cell to its previous valid value.
Press Ctrl+Z once and confirm the matched result reappears.

steps.action: Select the output cell for the two-way lookup beside your row-label and column-header input cells.
steps.where: Worksheet grid next to the two-way lookup inputs and source table.
steps.why: The result needs a dedicated cell that can respond to both lookup choices.
steps.checkpoint: The intended output cell has a green selection border.
hint_levels: Choose the cell where the row-and-column intersection should appear.
Use a blank cell near the two input cells so the relationship stays visible.
Click the blank result cell beside the row-label and column-header inputs.

steps.action: Enter a nested XLOOKUP that selects a table row first and then the requested column from that row.
steps.where: Formula bar above the worksheet grid.
steps.why: Nesting XLOOKUP performs a two-way lookup without hard-coded column numbers.
steps.checkpoint: The result cell displays the value at the intersection of the selected row and column.
hint_levels: Use the inner lookup to return an entire row, then search its headers.
Build =XLOOKUP(column_choice,header_range,XLOOKUP(row_choice,row_labels,data_body,"Not found"),"Not found").
In the result cell, type =XLOOKUP(column_input,header_range,XLOOKUP(row_input,row_label_range,data_range,"Not found"),"Not found") and press Enter.

steps.action: Change each two-way lookup input once and confirm the result updates to the new intersection.
steps.where: Row-label and column-header input cells in the worksheet grid.
steps.why: Testing both dimensions verifies that neither lookup is tied to a fixed row or column.
steps.checkpoint: The result changes after each input edit and matches the visibly intersecting source-table value.
hint_levels: Test the row choice and the column choice independently.
Pick another valid row label, then another valid header, and compare the result with the source table.
Click the row input, enter another listed row label, press Enter, then click the column input, enter another displayed header, and press Enter.
